pages.x: In the fifth century the Gupta emperors ruled most of northern India, in what is remembered as a golden age: the poet Kalidasa wrote his plays, mathematicians used the decimal numbers we use today, and the great Buddhist university at Nalanda was founded. Beyond the mountains to the north-west, a new people of the steppe, the Alchon Huns, had taken Kabul.

Around 460 the Huns pushed through the passes into India. The emperor Skandagupta led the Gupta army against them and drove them back, and his pillar at Bhitari boasts that the earth shook when he met the Hunas in battle. For a generation, they stayed beyond the Indus.

After Skandagupta died, quarrels over the throne weakened the empire. Around 500 the Hun king Toramana came down from Gandhara with his horsemen, overran the Punjab and reached Malwa, in the heart of India. An inscription on a great stone boar at Eran is dated in his reign.

Toramana's son Mihirakula ruled from Sakala, today's Sialkot, over lands from Kashmir to Gwalior. Buddhist writers remembered him as a monster who burned monasteries and killed monks, and a chronicle of Kashmir, written six centuries later, says he loved to hear the screams of elephants pushed over a cliff.

Around 520 a Chinese Buddhist pilgrim, Song Yun, came to the Hun court in Gandhara. He found a proud king who had been at war with Kashmir for three years, with hundreds of war elephants, and who received the Chinese emperor's letter without rising from his seat.

At last Indian kings joined against the Huns. Around 528 Yashodharman, king of Mandasor in Malwa, beat Mihirakula, and set up victory pillars saying that the Hun king had bowed at his feet. A later Chinese pilgrim gave the credit to a Gupta king, Narasimhagupta, who, he said, captured Mihirakula and let him go.

Mihirakula withdrew to Kashmir, and Hun power in India was broken. But so was the Gupta Empire, which split into rival kingdoms within a few decades, and India's classical age ended in a patchwork of regional states. Some historians think Hun settlers were among the ancestors of later warrior clans.
pts: Mihirakula ruled from Kashmir to Gwalior
